content: Biochemical tests of placental or feto-placental function were commonly utilized during the 1960s and 1970s in pregnancies considered high-risk. These tests aimed to predict adverse fetal outcomes and, by doing so, potentially prevent them. The objective of this study was to evaluate the impact of performing biochemical tests of placental function in pregnancies categorized as high-risk, low-risk, or unselected. To gather relevant data, a search was conducted within the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register on May 10, 2012. The study included controlled trials, either randomized or quasi-randomized, that compared the use of biochemical tests of placental function during pregnancy with the absence of such tests. The quality of the trials was assessed, and the data were extracted by the review author for analysis. Only one trial met the inclusion criteria, but it was of poor quality. This trial involved 622 women with high-risk pregnancies who underwent plasma (o)estriol estimations. Participants were assigned to either have their (o)estriol results disclosed or concealed, based on their hospital record number. This method of allocation introduced a potential risk of selection bias. The results showed no significant differences between the two groups in terms of perinatal mortality, with a relative risk (RR) of 0.88 and a 95% confidence interval (CI) ranging from 0.36 to 2.13. Similarly, there were no notable differences in the rates of planned delivery, with an RR of 0.97 and a 95% CI ranging from 0.81 to 1.15. The authors concluded that the available trial data do not support the use of (o)estriol estimation in high-risk pregnancies. The single small trial lacked sufficient power to rule out a potential beneficial effect. However, this finding is likely of historical interest only, as biochemical testing has largely been replaced by biophysical testing in the antepartum assessment of fetal well-being.
